title: Prefetch Thundering Herd: OOM Timeline and Mitigation (WIP)
content:
Short summary:

On 2026-03-10 02:18 UTC we observed a burst of OOMs in the GPU worker pool serving the v2 model family. The root trigger appears to be a prefetch/congestion interaction: an upstream traffic pattern changed (small increase in unique prefixes), which caused the prefetch subsystem to aggressively create many large KV cache prefetch tasks concurrently. Those prefetch tasks allocated transient CPU + host RAM for serialization and pinned a subset of GPU memory during warmup, which combined with continuous-batching changes from last week (longer batch windows) to cause memory pressure and eventual OOM kills on ~12 pods. Resulting fallout: request failures (5xx) for ~16 minutes, increased end-to-end latency for affected routes, and a fallback to hosted smaller-capacity clusters.

Impact:
- 12 GPU worker pods OOM-killed across two AZs in us-west-2
- ~16 minutes of elevated 5xx rate on /v1/generate and /v1/chat routes for customers using v2 models (SLO breach)
- One major customer observed latency spikes and temporarily enabled fallback config to a different shard

Immediate mitigation performed (timeline):
- 02:18 UTC: Alert fired (OOM rate anomaly). Ops routed to on-call SRE (Asha).
- 02:20 UTC: Scoped to serving-runtime v2 family using metric correlation (oom_count by pod, prefetch_task_queue_depth).
- 02:23 UTC: Killed inflight prefetch queue via feature-flag: PrefetchConcurrency=0 (feature flags service, rollout to affected clusters).
- 02:26 UTC: Scaled up control-plane eviction throttle to 3x to accelerate KV eviction and free host memory (temporary).
- 02:31 UTC: Rolled batch-window setting back to pre-2026-03-05 value for the affected deployment to reduce per-request in-memory resident state.
- 02:34 UTC: Gradually restarted OOM-killed pods with drain/recreate to restore capacity; monitored mem/resident metrics.
- 02:40 UTC: 5xx rate subsided to baseline. Continued monitoring until full recovery at 02:56 UTC.

Key evidence snippets:
- Metric correlations: prefetch_task_queue_depth spiked from ~20 -> ~950 across shard X in 90s. Concurrent prefetches per pod peaked at ~48 (threshold is 8).
- mem_used_host (worker) rose from median 18GB -> 46GB before OOM. JVM/py process reported large temporary buffers during kv prefetch serialization.
- continuous_batch_window: increased from 50ms -> 250ms by recent rollout (PR #1789) which increased KV cache live residency time per request.
- Sample log line: "[02:21:12 UTC] prefetcher: enqueue prefetch key=prefix=usr:session:abc size=9.8MB pid=1902"
- OOM reason from kernel dmesg: "OOM killer invoked: pid=1902 (worker) total_vm=2353412kB rss=452308kB"

Hypothesis / root cause (working):
1) Recent continuous-batching change increased the average window a request held KV references (longer lived KV cache contexts).
2) Prefetch heuristics kicked in on increased unique prefixes in traffic; the adaptive prefetcher ramped concurrency to try and warm lots of keys (we saw a bug where estimated cost per key was undercounted, leading to larger allocations than expected).
3) Prefetch tasks are not properly backpressured on host memory pressure; the concurrency limiter is token-based but tokens were not reclaimed promptly when tasks allocated large buffers (race between token release and exception path).
4) Combined memory usage (batch resident state + prefetch buffers + transient serialization) exceeded host limits and triggered OOM.

Why this wasn't caught earlier:
- Unit tests validate token accounting but not host-resident transient buffers; no e2e sim for simultaneous high prefetch + long batch-window.
- Observability lacked a high-cardinality metric: prefetch_memory_allocated_per_pod. We only had task counts.

Immediate runbook additions (short checklist to be applied today):
- Add emergency feature flag path to set PrefetchConcurrency=1 (we used 0 above when necessary) and test rollback plan. (owner: Asha)
- Add a temporary pod-level kube OOMScoreAdj on affected node pools to prefer restarting workers earlier (owner: Samir)
- Ensure CI job exists that simulates high unique-prefix traffic for prefetch heuristic testing (owner: Maya)
- Short-term: change default prefetch heuristic cap from 48 -> 8 (config PR queued: #1832 revert strategy)

Longer-term action items (postmortem/next cycle):
- Add metric prefetch_memory_allocated_per_pod and instrument allocator paths in prefetch service. Priority P0. (owner: Diego, ETA: 2 sprints)
- Implement strict memory-aware backpressure: prefetch tasks should consult host free memory and throttle. (owner: Serving-runtime team, ETA: 3 sprints)
- Rework token reclaim path to be synchronous on catastrophic allocation paths to avoid token leakage. (owner: Maya, ETA: 2 sprints)
- Add end-to-end test that exercises continuous-batching + prefetch concurrency under synthetic load and checks for memory safety (owner: infra QA, ETA: 1 sprint)
- Update rollout checklist: when changing continuous_batch_window, do canary with prefetch disabled; require metrics gating on prefetch_task_queue_depth and prefetch_memory_allocated. (owner: Product/Console, ETA: next release)

Repro steps (dev/test):
1) In test cluster, set continuous_batch_window=250ms and prefetch_heuristic_scale=high.
2) Run traffic generator script (repo: infra/testing/prefetch-loadgen) with unique_prefix_rate=800rps and concurrent_clients=300.
3) Observe prefetch_task_queue_depth -> should spike. Verify mem_used_host growth.
4) Disable prefetcher via feature flag to see the effect on 5xx and mem.

Emergency commands used (examples):
- Toggle feature flag: curl -X POST https://ff.redwood.internal/api/v1/flags/prefetch-concurrency -d '{"value":0}' -H 'Authorization: Bearer xxxxx'
- Revert batch window: kubectl -n serving set env deployment/worker-serving --containers=runtime --continuous_batch_window=50ms
- Force pod restart: kubectl -n serving rollout restart deployment/worker-serving --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node>

Open questions / unknowns:
- Why did token accounting not reflect transient large allocation? We need the allocator trace to find the code path.
- Was there any customer traffic pattern change we can detect upstream that correlates with new prefixes? (tracking: product events team)
- Are any other model families vulnerable (we saw shard X most impacted) because of different key-value size distributions?

Notes for runbook draft (proposed additions):
- Pre-incident checklist: Ensure "prefetch concurrency cap" and "prefetch memory metric" exist before any continuous-batching rollout.
- Detection rules: Alert when prefetch_task_queue_depth > 200 OR prefetch_concurrency_per_pod > 16 AND host_mem_used_percent > 70% for 30s.
- Immediate remediation steps: 1) flip feature flag prefetch -> 0, 2) scale down batch window to safe default, 3) increase eviction throttle, 4) restart affected pods gradually with draining, 5) notify customers via incident channel
- Postmortem criteria: If SLO breached > 5 minutes or >1 premium customer affected, escalate to Incident Review board for postmortem.

Follow-ups (owners assigned):
- Instrumentation: Diego (P0)
- Token reclaim patch: Maya (P1)
- Prefetch heuristic cap change and config: Samir (P0)
- E2E test for prefetch + batching: Infra QA (P0)
- Runbook update & gating for batch-window rollouts: Product (Rachel)

Appendix: quick excerpts from logs and dashboards (trimmed)
- prefetch queue spike chart: attached in linked_artifacts -> slack thread
- kube events: node/kubew-45 kernel OOM: pods/worker-abc killed at 02:24:11 UTC

Notes-to-self / informal:
- This incident feels like a classic resource accounting mismatch between planned token semantics and real transient allocations. The continuous-batching change increased the residency time of state in the worker which amplified impact. Prioritize adding host-aware backpressure; counting tasks is not enough.
- When pushing the token-reclaim change, include a stress-test harness that creates pathological key sizes so we don't regress.

Status: collecting allocator traces from affected pods (Diego), drafting token-reclaim PR (Maya), prefetched config rollback PR open (#1832). Will convert to a full postmortem if customer impact > 1 premium or SLO > 15m.
